data.name: The Godbeast
data.detailed_description:
The Godbeast blends atmospheric exploration and fast-paced melee combat in a stylish action/adventure. Set in a dark and timeless City, the banished Ysengrim returns from exile to take revenge for the murder of his father, the King.

The City's inhabitants have since been driven mad by the moonlight and worship the Council of the Hunt, cruel beings that keep the world trapped in an eternal nightmare. Their power is tied to the fate of the Godbeasts, divine animals that roam the streets.

Armed with an enchanted spear and riding his motorcycle, Ysengrim sets out to hunt down the giant Godbeasts and engage in fierce duels with the evil Lords that rule the City.

Key Features

  • Explore a mysterious and atmospheric City, with the ominous full moon in the night sky. Find action as well as rest in the dark shadows of the skyscrapers and the melancholic solitude of old forests.
  • Combine melee combat, spear throws, last-second evades and climbing in fast-paced battles with the monsters and beasts roaming the City streets. Drive your motorcycle straight into the fray and jump on the back of your enemies to deliver the killing blow.
  • Hunt and chase down the giant Godbeasts, mystical creatures that act as deities of the City. Weaken them with your spear, climb up their bodies and stab their weak points to drain their lifeblood away.

Credits

  • Designed & created by Jochen Mistiaen
  • Main title & key art by C. Bedford
  • Music & additional sound design by Fractures

reviews.review:
This game feels like much more of a proof of concept compared to the devs previous game Malebolgia, which was a very straightforward homage to classic horror games.
Course that doesn't mean your initial impression betrays you, this game wears its inspirations on its sleeve. Yes, this is very inspired by Shadow of the Colossus (and maybe a bit of Dragons Dogma). But the mazelike city, and enemies in the environment, soulslike bosses and mini-bosses are all a lot more experimental, particularly in the ways they come together in the central mechanic of the game.
Tracking.
The large beast that you are hunting move around should you fall, at which point you get back on your bike and find them. Killing enemies aligned to the one you're tracking will tell you the region they're in and from there, your spear will lead the way.
Its both were this game lives and dies. Its such a great idea and it really encourages learning the environment. And you would THINK that its an incentive to hold on as long as possible and do as much damage in one attempt. I'm unsure if I was just coincidentally unlucky or ignored a mechanic, but it seemed as though my best rounds of damage would be followed by repeated early flees from the beast. If I had to assume how the system worked, there are certain damage gates/flags that increases the beast aggression and should you pass multiple in one round, future attempts think you've already done damage and have fallen off? Or as said, the length of time the beast stays around is random and I'm reading far too much with my own luck. Personally its not a huge issue, but I imagine it could be confusing or frustrating to have attempts at the beast that end as soon as they begin. And, if it IS what I suspect about the damage flags, a lost opportunity to reward skill expression.
The rest of the games combat is a lot of fun, feeling a bit more aligned with a platinum games affair than say Souls, despite the ways the enemies themselves are designed. I have to say that the bosses in Malebolgia are all far more unique between eachother than the bosses on display here, and the inclusion of a ranged option fighting anything with all upgrades borders on power fantasy.
This is all what I mean by proof of concept. Certain aspects of the game seem geared for slow, atmospheric, methodical experience that's about overcoming odds. But the fluidity of the dodge roll, the power of throwing the spear, and the short fights lean more to character action. It feels intentional, and interesting, but perhaps conflicted.
It feels like a harder sell than Malebolgia. Not because its more or less interesting on its own, but because I feel like it'll be a person by person basis if you might fw this. It'll be WAY more interesting to some, or maybe atleast really chill to coast around the city on the bike. And to others, a short couple of fights with a lot of 'filler' inbetween getting lost time and time again in the city streets. But who cares, I fw it so its getting a recommendation.
Also I have no idea why there aren't street signs IN the environment. At 'highway' exits and crossing theres a popup at the bottom of the screen but its so hard to parse which direction is pointing especially at high speeds. Street signs would add some color to the environment AND be easier to read. Just a weird thing I thought about while tracking the last beast.
